common_name: February Silver Daffodil (Early White-and-Yellow Cyclamineus Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; February Silver is one of the earliest Cyclamineus daffodils to open, often ahead of the better-known February Gold.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. February Silver opens pale lemon buds that quickly fade to a crisp white perianth held behind a slender, clear yellow trumpet, giving a sharper color contrast than the all-yellow cultivars that share its early bloom time. The nodding, swept-back petals are typical of its Cyclamineus parentage and look best planted in drifts near the front of a bed where the flowers can be viewed at eye level. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after bloom so the bulbs can recharge for the following spring.

common_name: March Sunshine Daffodil (Multi-Headed Reflexed Yellow Cyclamineus Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; March Sunshine carries several small, reflexed yellow flowers per stem rather than the single bloom typical of most Cyclamineus hybrids.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil amended with compost. March Sunshine produces two or more small, deep yellow flowers per stem, each with petals swept back from a slim trumpet, giving a busier, more floriferous look than single-flowered Cyclamineus cultivars. It blooms a little later than the earliest dwarf daffodils, extending the display into the heart of spring, and naturalizes well when left undisturbed in a sunny, well-drained spot. Deadheading spent flowers tidies the planting but is not necessary for the bulbs to persist from year to year.

common_name: Snipe Daffodil (Miniature White Bulbocodium-Cyclamineus Hybrid Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Snipe is a dwarf daffodil bred from crosses between the hoop-petticoat and Cyclamineus groups.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil, as this miniature hybrid resents soggy conditions during its summer dormancy. Snipe produces creamy white flowers with a slender, flared cup and gently reflexed petals, blending the dwarf stature of its hoop-petticoat ancestry with the swept-back form inherited from Cyclamineus parents. Its small size makes it well suited to raised beds, troughs, and rock gardens rather than open borders. Allow the narrow foliage to fade completely before removing it to keep the bulbs vigorous for the next season.

common_name: Xit Daffodil (Miniature White Exhibition Small-Cup Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Xit is a miniature exhibition daffodil long favored by show growers for its pure white, flat form.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun. Xit opens flat, pure white flowers with a shallow, slightly frilled cup held on short, wiry stems, a combination that has made it a long-time favorite on the miniature daffodil show bench. Because of its diminutive scale it is best appreciated up close, in troughs, raised beds, or the very front edge of a rock garden rather than mixed among taller cultivars. Leave the foliage in place until it yellows naturally so the small bulbs can rebuild their reserves.

common_name: Pequenita Daffodil (Miniature Yellow-Fading-to-White Jonquilla Hybrid Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Pequenita is a Grant Mitsch-bred miniature jonquilla hybrid with multiple small flowers per stem.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. Pequenita bears clusters of small, rounded flowers that open bright yellow and gradually fade to a soft cream as they age, a two-tone effect that is most visible when several bulbs are massed together. As a jonquilla-type hybrid it tends to tolerate the hot, humid summers of warmer climates better than large trumpet daffodils, and it multiplies readily into dense clumps over time. Allow the slender foliage to die back on its own before cleaning up the bed.

common_name: Intrigue Daffodil (Fragrant Lemon-Yellow Jonquilla Hybrid Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Intrigue is a Grant Mitsch-bred jonquilla hybrid with a distinctive long, slender lemon-yellow cup.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Intrigue produces fragrant flowers with a pale lemon-yellow perianth surrounding a slim, trumpet-like cup of the same clear color that fades gently toward the rim as the bloom ages. The long, narrow cup form sets it apart from rounder-cupped jonquilla hybrids and makes a good cut flower for small arrangements. Like other jonquilla-type daffodils it generally perennializes well in warmer regions where large trumpet types struggle to return.

common_name: Stratosphere Daffodil (Multi-Headed Golden Yellow Jonquilla Hybrid Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Stratosphere carries several fragrant golden-yellow flowers on each tall stem, typical of robust jonquilla hybrids.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. Stratosphere sends up tall, sturdy stems topped with clusters of small, rounded, deep golden-yellow flowers that carry a noticeable fragrance, a scaled-up presentation compared to more compact jonquilla cultivars. The height and multi-flowered habit make it useful toward the middle or back of a mixed bulb border where it can be seen above shorter neighbors. As with other jonquilla hybrids, it tends to tolerate heat and humidity better than large trumpet daffodils and rewards being left undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Falstaff Daffodil (Golden Large-Cupped Daffodil with Red-Orange Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Falstaff is a Grant Mitsch-bred large-cupped daffodil noted for the rich, saturated color of its cup.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Falstaff opens broad, deep golden-yellow petals surrounding a large, flared cup that deepens to a rich red-orange, giving it strong presence in beds and borders from a distance. The sturdy stems and substantial flowers hold up well to spring wind and rain, and the cultivar has long been a popular choice among large-cupped daffodils grown for cutting and show. Leave the foliage to ripen fully after bloom so the bulbs can store energy for the following year.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Ambergate is a large-cupped daffodil valued for its unusually deep, warm coloring.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Ambergate carries burnt-orange petals and a darker, glowing red-orange cup, a warmer, more smoldering color combination than the typical yellow-and-orange large-cupped daffodil. The bold coloring stands out best against lighter companions such as white or pale yellow daffodils planted nearby. Allow the foliage to die back completely before removing it, since the bulbs rely on it to build strength for next spring's bloom.

common_name: Vulcan Daffodil (Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Orange-Red Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Vulcan is a long-cultivated large-cupped daffodil bred in Northern Ireland.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Vulcan bears clear yellow petals surrounding a broad, flat-faced cup banded in fiery orange-red, a reliable and long-popular combination for borders and cut-flower use. Its sturdy constitution and consistent flowering have kept it in circulation among large-cupped daffodils for decades even as newer cultivars have been introduced. Let the foliage yellow and collapse naturally after bloom rather than cutting or tying it, so the bulbs can recharge for next season.

common_name: Goldfinger Daffodil (Large Golden Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Goldfinger is a Grant Mitsch-bred trumpet daffodil known for its large, well-proportioned bloom.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Goldfinger produces a single, substantial golden-yellow flower per stem, with a long, slightly flared trumpet in strong proportion to its broad petals, giving it classic show-quality form. The large flowers and sturdy stems make it a good choice for cutting as well as for massed display in beds and borders. Leave the strap-like foliage in place until it fades on its own so the bulb can store energy for next year's flower.

common_name: Golden Ducat Daffodil (Double Golden Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Golden Ducat is a sport of a classic golden trumpet daffodil, fully doubled into a solid pompom of petals.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Golden Ducat produces a fully double flower built from layers of ruffled, solid golden-yellow petals rather than a distinct trumpet and cup, giving a rounded, peony-like bloom on a sturdy stem. The dense petal count makes it a favorite for both garden display and forcing indoors over winter. Stake taller stems in exposed, windy spots, since the heavy double flowers can weigh the stem down more than single-flowered trumpet types.

common_name: Rose of May Daffodil (Historic Double White Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Rose of May is an old double white daffodil long grown as a cottage-garden pass-along plant.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil enriched with compost, in full sun to light shade. Rose of May produces fully double, creamy white flowers made up of many narrow, slightly twisted petals, giving each bloom a loose, frilled appearance quite different from the flatter doubles bred more recently. As an old heirloom cultivar it has a long history of being passed from garden to garden and tends to be dependable once established in a spot with good drainage. Allow the foliage to die back completely each year, since repeated early cutting weakens the bulbs over time.

common_name: Quince Daffodil (Fragrant Soft Yellow Jonquilla Hybrid Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Quince is a Grant Mitsch-bred jonquilla hybrid with soft, pastel-yellow flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs 5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. Quince carries small, fragrant flowers in a soft, muted yellow that is gentler than the bright gold typical of many jonquilla hybrids, with a shallow, slightly darker cup at the center. Its moderate height and mild coloring make it easy to tuck among other spring bulbs without overpowering them. Like other jonquilla-type daffodils, it generally handles heat and humidity well and can be left undisturbed for years to form larger clumps.

common_name: Printal Daffodil (White Split-Corona Daffodil with Orange-Red Collar)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Printal is a split-corona daffodil whose flattened cup opens against the petals like a collar.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Printal has a pure white perianth behind a corona that is split and spread flat against the petals, striped and edged in orange-red so the whole flower reads almost like a single layered disc rather than a traditional trumpet-and-petal form. This flattened, collar-like corona is the hallmark of split-corona daffodils and gives the flower strong impact in beds viewed from above, such as along a path. Allow the foliage to ripen and yellow fully before removing it to keep the bulbs blooming well in future years.

common_name: Birma Daffodil (Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Flat Orange-Red Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; Birma is a long-grown Dutch large-cupped daffodil popular for bedding and forcing.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Birma carries bright yellow petals around a short, flat-faced cup edged in deep orange-red, a crisp two-tone combination that reads well from a distance in mass bedding displays. It has long been grown commercially both as a garden bulb and for early indoor forcing, owing to its reliable, uniform flowering. After bloom, let the foliage die back naturally in place so the bulbs can build reserves for the next growing season.
